## A morning that starts with the wrong question

You stand in a grocery aisle holding two boxes. One says *English Breakfast*. One says *sencha*. Both are "tea." Both will wake you up a little. Yet one will pour dark and malty, the other pale and grassy—and the calm-focus side of the cup will not feel the same.

Most people ask, "Which brand is better?" A better first question is quieter: **which plant style am I holding—and what did the factory do to it?** This lesson answers the plant half. Processing, brewing, and the three named guests come in the sittings that follow. If aisle labels still feel foggy, skim **[Tea basics](../../tea-basics.qmd)** first, then come back.

::: {.callout-tip title="Words to know in this sitting"}
- **Camellia sinensis** — the tea plant species behind almost all commercial tea.
- **China type (var. *sinensis*)** — smaller-leaved, cooler-hill style on average.
- **Assam type (var. *assamica*)** — larger-leaved, warm-lowland style on average.
- **Polyphenols / catechins** — plant compounds that shape astringency and, later, black-tea pigments.
- **L-theanine** — a calming amino acid often higher in China-type dry leaf on average.
:::

## Two plants, one species

Commercial tea is *Camellia sinensis*. Think of it as one species with two main "flavors" of plant, the way dogs are one species with many breeds. Botanists have argued for decades about how to name those forms. A classic *Nature* note by W. Wight sorted the naming problem for tea taxonomists and still sits behind how growers talk about China-type and Assam-type plants.[^1]

The **China type** (var. *sinensis*) tends to be a smaller-leaved shrub. It grows more slowly and handles cold better. It is often linked with cooler, higher hills. The **Assam type** (var. *assamica*) tends to be larger-leaved and more tree-like. It grows faster in warm, humid lowlands.[^2][^3]

Why should a drinker care? Because dry-leaf chemistry differs on average. Assam-type leaves often carry more caffeine and more polyphenols (a big family of plant compounds). China-type leaves often carry more L-theanine. Growing conditions and which leaf you pick still matter a lot—so averages are guides, not laws.[^4][^5]

Picture a small, hardy bush on a cool hillside versus a larger, leafy plant in a hot lowland garden. That contrast is the China-type vs Assam-type story. One careful survey of world cultivars found that the Assam group showed the widest spread in tannin (polyphenol) and caffeine, and that cultivars with especially high tannin (above about 25% dry weight) appeared only in the Assam group—useful breeding material, and a reminder that "Assam" is not a single cookie-cutter plant.[^4]

The draft genome of *Camellia sinensis* var. *sinensis* also helps explain why flavor chemistry is not a marketing slogan: the plant's evolutionary path left it unusually rich in pathways that make caffeine, theanine, and catechins—the same three families Chapter 1 keeps returning to.[^8]

## A drinker's comparison table

The table below puts typical dry-leaf ranges from the source packs in one place so you can see the pattern at a glance.

| | China type (var. *sinensis*) | Assam type (var. *assamica*) | Source trail |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Leaf style | Smaller leaves | Larger leaves | Barua (1989)[^2] |
| Growth | Slower shrub, about 1–3 m; more cold-tolerant | Faster tree-like plant, about 8–15 m; prefers warm climates | Wight (1959); Mondal (2014)[^1][^3] |
| Typical leaf area | About 15–40 cm² | About 50–150 cm² | Mondal (2014)[^3] |
| Cold limit (rough) | Can survive about −15°C to −20°C | Damage often below about −5°C | Ban et al. (2017)[^7] |
| Polyphenols (dry leaf) | About 15%–25% | About 25%–35% | Borchetia et al. (2009); Takeda (1994)[^5][^4] |
| L-theanine (dry leaf) | Often higher (about 1.5%–3.0%) | Often moderate (about 0.5%–1.5%) | Wei et al. (2018)[^8] |
| Caffeine (dry leaf) | About 2.0%–3.5% | About 3.5%–5.5% | Ashihara et al. (2008); Takeda (1994)[^9][^4] |
| Typical growing area | Cooler, higher hills | Warm, humid lowlands | Carr (2018); packs |

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="More detail: what the cultivar survey actually measured"}
Takeda's 1994 Japan Agricultural Research Quarterly survey compared caffeine and tannin across tea cultivars used in breeding.[^4] Mean caffeine sat near **4.09%** dry weight for Assam-group material versus about **3.11%** for China-group material—a real average gap, not a guarantee for any one garden. The same survey's high-tannin (above ~25% dry weight) outliers appeared only in the Assam group, which is why breeders still mine *assamica* when they want polyphenol punch.

A separate East African clonal study under matched field design likewise found Assam-type clones richer in catechins and total polyphenols than chinary types—useful because it holds growing site roughly constant.[^6]

**What this does *not* say:** your supermarket "Assam" blend is not a single genotype. Blending, plucking standard (two leaves and a bud vs coarser leaf), shade, and fertilizer can move caffeine by percentage points. The pack narrative already notes a shaded, well-fed China-type bud near **4.5%** caffeine and a poorly fed mature Assam leaf near **2.5%**. Averages lean Assam-higher; gardens write the fine print.
:::

## The myth of "Assam always doubles China caffeine"

Here is a common story people tell: "Assam always has far more caffeine." Average figures often put *assamica* higher—Takeda's cultivar survey reported Assam-group mean caffeine around 4.09% versus about 3.11% for China-group material[^4]—but growing conditions and which leaf you pick matter a lot. A well-fed, shaded China-type bud can reach about 4.5% caffeine; a poorly fed mature Assam leaf can sit near 2.5% (pack narrative ranges). So "Assam = double caffeine" is too blunt.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="More detail: the garden dials that rewrite averages"}
Three dials move dry-leaf chemistry as much as variety labels do:

1. **Which leaf you pick.** Young buds and the first leaves are usually richer in caffeine and amino acids than older, coarser leaf. "Two leaves and a bud" is not poetry—it is a plucking standard that changes the cup.
2. **Shade and nitrogen.** Shading (famous in Japanese Gyokuro and tencha for matcha) and generous feeding can lift L-theanine and, in some settings, caffeine in China-type material. That is one reason a shaded China-type bud can out-caffeine a neglected Assam leaf in the pack's counter-example.
3. **Blending.** Grocery "Assam" or "English Breakfast" is often a blend across gardens and seasons. The label names a *style*, not a single bush.

Cold hardiness is another quiet dial: Ban and colleagues' transcriptome work on cold acclimation helps explain why China-type bushes survive colder hills while Assam-type material prefers warmer basins.[^7] Caffeine biosynthesis reviews (Ashihara and colleagues) keep the biochemical map of how the plant makes the stimulant in the first place.[^9]
:::

## Why this plant story matters for black tea later

And there is one more plant-to-cup thread worth remembering for later: higher catechin levels in *assamica* give more raw material for the dark pigments of black tea. That is why Assam-type leaves are such a natural fit for strong black-tea processing—a bridge we will meet again on the [Linkages](../../linkages.qmd) page and in [Lesson 1.2](02-processing.qmd). East African clonal work likewise often finds Assam-type material richer in catechins and total polyphenols than chinary types under the same field design.[^6]

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="More detail: mapping plants to aisle words"}
Quick bridges to everyday labels (full map in [Tea basics](../../tea-basics.qmd)):

- **English Breakfast / Assam breakfast blends** — often lean Assam-type leaf and black processing; expect malt, body, and a more familiar caffeine feel.
- **Sencha / many Chinese greens** — often China-type leaf with heat that *stops* browning early; expect grassy/vegetal notes and more intact catechins.
- **Matcha / Gyokuro** — usually shaded China-type material; L-theanine can climb; matcha also means you ingest the leaf powder, not only an infusion.
- **Herbal "tea"** — usually *not* *Camellia sinensis* (peppermint, rooibos, chamomile). Different plant, different chemistry.

None of those label shortcuts replace reading the tin—but they stop the aisle from feeling random.
:::

## What to take from this sitting

- Almost all commercial tea is one species with two main plant styles.
- Averages lean Assam-higher for caffeine and polyphenols, China-higher for L-theanine—**gardens rewrite the fine print**.
- Higher catechin raw material in Assam-type leaf is one reason strong black tea loves that plant style.
- Aisle words are shortcuts; [Tea basics](../../tea-basics.qmd) and the [Cup reference](../../cup-reference.qmd) keep labels and milligrams honest.

So far we have the leaf on the bush. Next comes the factory choice that decides whether that leaf stays green or turns dark.


## Story in one minute

One species. Two main plant styles. China-type bushes lean cooler hills, smaller leaves, and—on average—more L-theanine. Assam-type plants lean warm lowlands, larger leaves, and—on average—more caffeine and polyphenols. Your supermarket tin may ignore all of that and still taste wonderful, because gardens, plucking, shade, and blends rewrite averages. The point of this sitting is not to memorize a passport for every leaf. It is to stop treating "tea" as one chemical object.

## What this means when you drink tea

- If you want a calmer-focus leaning cup, China-type greens and shaded styles are a smarter *starting bet* than a bargain Assam breakfast bag—then still check the [Cup reference](../../cup-reference.qmd).
- If you want malt and punch, Assam-type black processing has the plant chemistry on its side.
- If someone insists Assam always doubles China caffeine, you now have Takeda's averages *and* the garden counter-examples.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="More detail: a worked 'two boxes' example"}
**Box A — English Breakfast.** Often Assam-leaning leaf + black oxidation. Expect theaflavins/thearubigins (from [Lesson 1.2](02-processing.qmd)), familiar caffeine feel, usually modest L-theanine in a quick steep ([Lesson 1.3](03-brewing.qmd)).

**Box B — Sencha.** Often China-type leaf + early heat kill. Expect monomeric catechins preserved, grassy liquor, and a different EGCG-to-caffeine balance if you brew near ~80°C.

Same word on the shelf ("tea"). Different plant-style *tendencies* plus different processing forks. That is why Module 1 is four sittings, not one paragraph.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Click for more detail: take-home checklist for Lesson 1.1"}
1. Species first: *Camellia sinensis* almost always.[^1]
2. Style second: China-type vs Assam-type averages.[^4]
3. Garden third: pluck, shade, feed, blend.
4. Aisle fourth: [Tea basics](../../tea-basics.qmd) for labels.
5. Milligrams fifth: [Cup reference](../../cup-reference.qmd) before Module 2 claims.
:::
